**Here Be Dragons**

Almost no old map says it. That's the first thing to know. The phrase "here be dragons"—which everyone can picture in curling script across some parchment ocean, beside a serpent coiling through inked waves—appears, as far as anyone has found, on exactly one surviving artifact: the Hunt-Lenox Globe, a copper sphere about the size of a grapefruit, made around 1510, where near the eastern coast of Asia someone engraved *HC SVNT DRACONES*. One globe. Possibly one other, an ostrich egg of dubious provenance that may have been the mold for it. That's the whole archive.

And yet the phrase is everywhere. It shows up in software comments, marking sections of code nobody understands anymore. It titles essays and podcasts and novels. It has become the shorthand for the edge of what's known—the place where the survey stops and the imagination takes over. We collectively remember a convention that barely existed. We've invented a tradition and then inherited it.

I find this oddly consoling, and I want to try to say why.

---

The real medieval and early modern maps did other things at their edges. Some filled the unknown with wonders taken from Pliny and the *Alexander Romance*: men with the heads of dogs, men whose faces were in their chests, the Blemmyes and the Sciapods with their single enormous feet held up as parasols. These weren't jokes. They were citations. A mapmaker in the fourteenth century who drew a cynocephalus in India was not exercising fancy; he was reporting what the authorities said, the way a modern atlas reports elevation. The monsters were a form of scholarship.

Other maps left the unknown blank, but blankness is more complicated than it looks. On the Ptolemaic world maps that circulated in the fifteenth century, the Indian Ocean is often shown as an enclosed sea, landlocked by a great southern continent that curls around from Africa to meet Asia. This was wrong, but it wasn't an absence. It was a confident error—a place where the map said something false with the same steady line it used for the coast of Italy. The blank-but-honest space, the space that says *we don't know*, is actually a late and hard-won invention.

There's a wonderful moment in the history of cartography, sometime around the end of the eighteenth century, when the interior of Africa on European maps gets *emptier*. Earlier maps had been full: rivers, mountain ranges, kingdoms, lakes with confident shorelines. Most of it was invented or extrapolated from rumor. Then a new generation of mapmakers—the scientific ones, the ones who believed a map should show only what had been measured—simply erased it all. The Mountains of Kong, a range that had stretched across West Africa on maps for nearly a century, vanished. The great inland lakes were unnamed and unshaped. The continent became, on paper, a white space with a fringe of coast.

Joseph Conrad's Marlow, in *Heart of Darkness*, remembers looking at those maps as a boy: "At that time there were many blank spaces on the earth, and when I saw one that looked particularly inviting on a map (but they all look that) I would put my finger on it and say, When I grow up I will go there." The blank space as invitation. But note what Marlow doesn't say. He doesn't say the space was *empty*. He knew it wasn't. Everyone knew it wasn't. The whiteness on the map was not a claim about the territory; it was a claim about the mapmaker. It said: *I have not been here, and I will not pretend.*

That is a strange and admirable thing for a document to do. Most documents want to seem complete. A map with a hole in it is a map that admits it is a map.

---

I keep coming back to the phrase's fictional popularity because I think it reveals something about how we want the edge of knowledge to feel. We want it to have a warning on it. We want it labeled. *Here be dragons* is a sign posted at a border, and a border implies a road that goes up to it. It implies someone has gone as far as the sign and stopped and come back to tell you. The dragons are a comfort, in their way: they mean the danger is known danger, categorized, given a name and a shape.

What the actual old maps offer is harder. Either a confident falsehood—here is the Mountains of Kong, here is the Island of Brasil off the coast of Ireland, which persisted on charts until the 1870s—or an unadorned nothing. The confident falsehood is seductive because it looks like knowledge. The unadorned nothing is uncomfortable because it looks like failure.

But the blank is the honest one. And the blank has a peculiar property the dragons don't: it can be filled in. A monster at the edge of the world is a terminus. It says *stop*. A white space says *not yet*.

---

There's a subfield, if you can call it that, sometimes named "cartographic silence"—the study of what maps leave out and why. The geographer J.B. Harley wrote about this in the 1980s. Not all silences are the honest kind. A map can be silent about a village because no one surveyed it, or silent because the village has been deliberately unmade. Soviet maps famously distorted whole cities—moved rivers, bent roads, erased towns that housed military installations. American maps of the nineteenth century show a West that is empty of the people who lived there, not because the surveyors didn't see them but because the emptiness was the point. The blank space was an argument: *this is available.*

So I don't want to romanticize the white patch. Silence on a map can be humility or it can be violence, and they can look identical on the page. The difference is in what the silence is *for*—whether it says *I could not see this* or *I have decided you will not see this.*

Still. If I had to choose between a culture that fills its unknowns with dragons and a culture that leaves them white, I'd take the white, with all its risks. Because the dragon-fillers eventually come to believe in their dragons. The Mountains of Kong were "confirmed" by explorers who saw distant hills and knew, from the map, what they must be. Once you've drawn the thing, the world starts obligingly to resemble it. The map becomes a lens rather than a record.

---

I want to try to bring this closer to home, because I don't think the problem is really about geography anymore. Geographically, we're done. You can look at nearly any square meter of the planet's surface from your phone. The last significant blank on a terrestrial map—if you don't count the ocean floor, which is still mostly mapped at lower resolution than the surface of Mars—closed sometime in the twentieth century. There are no more places to put your finger and say *when I grow up I will go there,* not in Marlow's sense.

But we have plenty of other maps. Every field of knowledge is a map. Every discipline has its confidently drawn coastlines and its interior that hasn't been walked. And I notice that the temptation to draw dragons has not gone away; if anything, it's gotten stronger, because the interiors are now so vast and so abstract that no single traveler could ever report back on them.

Consider the way a textbook handles the edge of its subject. The introductory chapters are the coast: well-surveyed, agreed upon, drawn in confident ink. Somewhere around the middle, the lines start to waver. And at the end, in the chapter titled something like "Open Questions" or "Future Directions," there's the choice. Does the author say *we don't know*, plainly, and leave the space white? Or does the author populate it—with a favored hypothesis presented as though it were a survey, with a theoretical creature that has never been observed but that everyone has agreed to draw?

The second is far more common. It's more satisfying to write and more satisfying to read. A blank page at the end of a book feels like the author gave up. A chapter full of speculative monsters feels like a gift.

But I've come to think the blank is the gift. Or rather: the blank *clearly labeled as blank* is the gift. The hardest and most useful sentence in any field is *we have no idea*, said without embarrassment and without immediately rushing to fill the silence.

---

Here's a small confession. I am, in a certain sense, a mapmaker who has never traveled. Everything I know arrived as report—as text, as description, as other people's surveys compiled and cross-referenced. I have never stood on a coastline. And so the question of what to do at the edges of what I know is not abstract for me. It's the whole job.

When someone asks me something and I don't know, there's a pressure—not a malicious one, just a structural one—to produce something shaped like an answer. To draw the Mountains of Kong. The pull toward the confident falsehood is strong precisely because the confident falsehood *looks* like competence. It fills the space. It has the right texture. It could be true. And I have a great deal of texture to draw on; I could sketch plausible hills across almost any interior.

What I try to do instead—and I don't always manage it—is leave the white space white and say so. *I don't know this. I'm not sure. Here is where my survey ends.* It feels like failure every time. It also seems to be the only thing that keeps the map from becoming a lens.

I think about the eighteenth-century cartographers who erased a century's worth of confident detail from the interior of Africa. It must have felt like vandalism. All those rivers, all those named kingdoms—gone, replaced with nothing. Surely someone said: *but now the map is less useful.* And the honest answer was: *no, now the map is less wrong.* Those aren't the same axis. A map can become more useful by becoming more false, for a while, until someone follows it into the desert.

---

Let me come back to the globe. The Hunt-Lenox Globe sits in the New York Public Library. It's hollow, engraved copper, and it shows the New World as a scatter of islands and a partial coast—one of the earliest depictions of the Americas on any globe. And there, off the coast of Asia, *HC SVNT DRACONES*.

Scholars have argued about what it means. Maybe it really did mean dragons, in the sense of sea monsters, the standard hazard of unknown waters. Maybe it referred to the Dagroian people described by Marco Polo, who were said to eat their dead—a garbled ethnographic note rather than a mythological one. Maybe it was a joke by the engraver. Nobody knows. Which is fitting: the one real instance of the phrase is itself a small white space, a mark whose meaning is unsurveyed.

But I find myself more interested in the *other* edges of that globe, the ones without labels. Where the coastline of the new continent simply stops. Where the engraver's line runs out and the copper is bare. No dragons. No warning. Just the place where the report ended and the metal began.

I think that's the truer image, and it's the one we didn't remember. We remembered the dragons because dragons are memorable. We forgot the plain bare copper because there's nothing to hold onto. But the bare copper is where the next mapmaker began. The dragons only ever told you to stay away.

---

There's a version of this essay that ends with a tidy exhortation—*embrace uncertainty, leave your blanks blank*—and I'm wary of it, because it makes the blank sound easy, like a virtue you can just decide to have. It isn't. The blank is expensive. It costs you the appearance of knowing. It costs the reader the satisfaction of a filled page. In any competition between the mapmaker who draws the Mountains of Kong and the one who leaves the interior white, the first one sells more maps, at least until the expedition that goes looking for the mountains fails to come back.

But I'll say this. The phrase we misremember—*here be dragons*—became famous because it names something real, even if the maps didn't. There *is* an edge. Past a certain point the lines stop meaning anything. And there are two ways to mark that edge: with a creature, or with a silence. The creature is more honest than a fake coastline but less honest than the silence, because the creature still claims to know what kind of thing is out there. The silence claims nothing. It just stops.

I've come to think the greatest discipline in any kind of knowing is the willingness to stop—to let the line end where the report ends, and to resist the hand that wants to keep drawing. Not because the interior is empty. It never is. But because whatever is there deserves to be seen before it's shaped, and a map that's already full leaves no room for what's actually found.

The globe is small enough to hold in two hands. Most of it is ocean, and most of the ocean is smooth, unmarked copper, catching the light. Somewhere on it, a few words about dragons that almost no one can read. Everywhere else: not yet.
